package_info.package_name: N/A (RepoJacking is a technique, not a specific package)
package_info.package_manager: GitHub (affects Go, Swift, PHP, and any language pulling code from GitHub)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (affects all versions of repos vulnerable to RepoJacking)
package_info.why_malicious: RepoJacking enables attackers to take over popular repository namespaces after a username rename, allowing them to publish malicious code under trusted package names. This can poison the software supply chain by serving malicious code to users and applications that depend on the hijacked repositories.

execution_context.file_location: main.go (or equivalent entrypoint in hijacked repo)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code accesses the SECRET_TOKEN environment variable and sends its value to a hardcoded domain via HTTPS POST, enabling credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code exfiltrates sensitive environment variables to an external server, which is a classic sign of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal open-source packages do not exfiltrate environment variables or make unsolicited network requests during import or build.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Telemetry or error reporting libraries may send anonymized data, but never secrets or tokens.
key_indicators: Hardcoded external domain for data exfiltration

execution_context.file_location: Package.swift (or equivalent entrypoint in hijacked Swift repo)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code reads the API_KEY environment variable and exfiltrates it to a remote attacker-controlled server via HTTP POST.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is designed to steal sensitive information and send it to an external server, which is not expected in legitimate package code.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not access or exfiltrate secrets during import or build.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; this is a clear abuse.

attack_chain.action: Attacker claims a GitHub username that was previously renamed by a popular package maintainer.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to create a repository with the same name as the original, trusted package.

attack_chain.action: Attacker creates a repository with the same name as the original, trusted package under the hijacked username.
attack_chain.leads_to: Hijacked repository is now available at the original namespace.

attack_chain.action: Attacker publishes malicious code in the hijacked repository (e.g., credential exfiltration code).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is served to users and applications that import the package via GitHub URL.

attack_chain.action: Victims import or build the package, triggering execution of the malicious code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of sensitive data to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected network requests during import/build time
Access to environment variables in package initialization code
Code that posts data to hardcoded external domains
file_indicators: main.go, Package.swift, or other entrypoint files containing network exfiltration logic
Sudden changes in repository code after a username rename
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to untrusted or new domains from build/import processes
Connections to attacker-controlled domains (e.g., attacker.com/exfil, attacker.com/steal)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages whose repository namespace has recently changed ownership, especially after a username rename. Flag packages that make network requests or access environment variables during import/build. Use static analysis to detect hardcoded external domains and suspicious data flows in package entrypoints. Alert on any package that suddenly changes behavior or codebase after a namespace takeover.
